title: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
desc: Describes contextual systems built with lawyer–engineer collaboration, predominantly operating as verified copilots rather than autonomous services.

kps.k: Generative AI expands the range of legal work that software can address.
kps.d: The substantive proposition is that large language models make unstructured, language-intensive work—drafting, summarisation, research, contract review, diligence and information extraction—more tractable than earlier rules-based or extraction systems. Builders often identify GPT-4 as the commercial threshold. These claims explain the breadth of experimentation but rely mainly on demonstrations and development experience; they do not establish uniform performance across tasks or practice areas.

qs.q: However, like legal work was largely immune to this because lawyers deal with unstructured text and computers just up until great LLMs, like computers were not good at reading unstructured text or outputting it.
qs.a: E38 - How Will SaaSpocalypse Affect AI For Legal: Spellbook CEO Scott Stevenson · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: But yeah, I would say GPT-4 then as I mentioned earlier, was probably the starting gun for the industry.
qs.a: E39 - AI vs Legacy SaaS in Legal: Min-Kyu Jung, CEO Ivo · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: The central product dispute concerns whether legal-specific workflow layers can remain valuable as general models improve.
kps.d: General-model advocates argue that frontier platforms increasingly reproduce specialist features and lower the cost of building alternatives. Legal-AI vendors locate differentiation in authoritative and client-specific data, citations, document handling, permissions, security, matter context, evaluation and integration with existing systems. A related unresolved question is whether broad horizontal assistants or narrow workflow products will capture more durable value. The disagreement concerns the surrounding product and infrastructure rather than whether specialist vendors rely on foundation models.

qs.q: Because I think, I think what you’re highlighting with the data that you’re showing, and I say this as a legal technology entrepreneur who builds apps and is regularly asked, What does this do that ChatGPT can’t do right?
qs.a: Front-Stabbing the Future: AI, Law, and the Global Unraveling of Rules with Sean West · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: Um, and then I think the part that we've built around is like if you use chat GPT or any of these basic language models to do programming, legal, any like complex knowledge work, you really quickly run into the edges whether it's not connected to my data, it's not connected to the systems I use, it doesn't have some of the expertise that I need.
qs.a: Gabe Pereyra — Harvey: 'the models are the product', ROI, and turning firm expertise into saleable models · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

kps.k: Builders emphasise contextual, task-specific systems and close lawyer–engineer collaboration.
kps.d: Many providers favour model-agnostic architectures that select different foundation models by task and combine them with retrieval, structured legal relationships, institutional knowledge and persistent client or matter context. They also argue that practising lawyers must help map workflows, encode risk preferences and assess wording and deliverables. Legal-only training faces constraints from limited or inaccessible data, while retrieval and customisation can improve relevance without eliminating hallucinations or proving reliability. The organisational claims rest largely on operating experience rather than controlled comparisons.

qs.q: Having some data model that looks at how cases have an effect on each other, where it might not be obvious to pull that out of an LLM, but having those two things work together make for something that’s really powerful.
qs.a: Preventing Harm Amidst the AI Hype — full episode transcript · Access to justice · 2025

qs.q: **John Sarihan:** Yeah, I think what we found is the state of the art is not specifically tuned for contracts because there’s not enough data in the corpus out there.
qs.a: Deal Velocity, Not Billable Hours: How Crosby Uses AI to Redefine Legal Contracting — publisher's transcript · AI-native providers · 2025

kps.k: Current deployment predominantly follows a copilot model with human verification and professional accountability.
kps.d: Providers commonly use AI to prepare drafts, analyses, issue lists or routed work while lawyers direct the task, verify outputs, exercise judgment and approve escalation. This verification work is distinct from benchmarking model performance. Agentic systems may eventually plan and execute more multi-step work with limited supervision, but permissioning, hallucinations, confidentiality and liability constrain movement toward autopilot. Some providers pursue higher automation only for bounded work and retain lawyers or regulated supervision for approval and accountability.

qs.q: you still have to kind of review the work and tell them what to do, but once you do, you've got this basically legal AI, this analytical power that you can point at whatever it is that you need to point  it at to get your job done.
qs.a: Cecilia Ziniti — GC AI (Founder & CEO, former General Counsel) · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: I mean, as an attorney, you're always going to be responsible for your own work product.
qs.a: Sean Fitzpatrick — LexisNexis (CEO, North America/UK/Ireland) on Protégé, the OpenAI Agreement and Augmentation Not Replacement · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

kps.k: Adoption depends on workflow fit, governance and organisational incentives as much as model capability.
kps.d: Large firms can fund pilots but may struggle with partner autonomy, fragmented practices and firm-wide uptake. In-house legal departments may align more readily around common workflows and business outcomes, although the evidence is organisation-specific rather than representative. Reported implementation practices include embedding tools where lawyers already work, deploying in phases, establishing safe-use rules, training users, demonstrating value on real matters and iterating through practitioner feedback. Proposed controls address trust and risk, but the material rarely demonstrates that they prevent harm in operation.

qs.q: And I think the other thing that I saw in working with the biggest law firms at McKinsey was that it's actually very hard to get high adoption rates and to get everyone to buy into a single system or tool.
qs.a: How AI Is Reshaping In-House Legal Teams with Nick Fleisher — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: And I think the underlying thing was our belief, both me and my sister, Mariam, uh as founders, has always been that legal AI works best when your context and your legal document meets the lawyers where they already work.
qs.a: From Customer to Acquirer: Filevine's Ryan Anderson and Pincites' Sona Sulakian on Building AI Contract Intelligence · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Providers disagree over whether transformation will come from software sold to lawyers or AI-native businesses delivering legal work.
kps.d: Software vendors position AI as infrastructure or assistance for incumbent firms and legal departments. AI-native law firms and service providers argue that clients often want completed, accountable outcomes rather than another tool, and that operating the service reveals the full workflow needed for deeper automation. These businesses seek to redesign intake, substantive work, administration and client support while accepting malpractice responsibility or regulated supervision. Critics note that combining a technology company with a law firm creates execution complexity, while incumbents retain advantages in relationships and accumulated work product.

qs.q: We didn't want to build an LPO, but we understood viscerally that companies want a faster, cheaper, and  reliable legal service rather than some AI platform that plugs into their word document.
qs.a: Ryan Daniels — Crosby (AI-native law firm) · AI-native providers · 2025

qs.q: We were building a law firm around how uh AI and and software uh uh works.
qs.a: Pierre Proner — Lawhive on walking away from SaaS and buying law firms instead · AI-native providers · 2026

kps.k: The commercial thesis extends beyond time savings to workflow redesign and different service economics.
kps.d: Proponents argue that efficiency alone can conflict with hourly billing and partnership incentives. They instead emphasise faster turnaround, increased capacity, fixed-fee or outcome-oriented offerings, self-service and automation of non-billable operations. In-house orchestration and AI-native delivery could reduce some routine outside-counsel work, but complex and high-risk matters remain less amenable to automation. Earlier legal-tech challengers’ limited disruption and the commoditisation of basic extraction qualify claims that current investment or adoption will produce durable structural change.

qs.q: But if you can't do that, um, efficiency is is  a hard cell unless you can convince them that there are ways for them to actually transform their business, right?
qs.a: Winston Weinberg (Harvey) — Sequoia Training Data Ep.33 · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: So it's really hard for them to allocate money that they could take home today um to long-term innovation.
qs.a: Ryan Daniels — Crosby (AI-native law firm) · AI-native providers · 2025

kps.k: Reported operational gains are promising but do not establish a settled comparative case.
kps.d: The evidence includes a narrow attorney-reviewed Harvey exercise, vendor-reported time savings, active-user rates, contract-review turnaround and faster development of extraction fields. These measures address acceptability, maximum reported savings, usage, processing time or development speed—not general legal accuracy, average productivity, error rates or client outcomes. Much of the remaining support comes from customer anecdotes, demonstrations and positive practitioner impressions without disclosed baselines or independent evaluation. Practical assessment should therefore define the workflow and measure quality, cost, turnaround, human touch points and escalation rates separately.

qs.q: We just said, “A potential customer asked this question, here’s the answer — would you make any edits or would you send this as is?” On 86 of the 100 samples, two out of three attorneys or more said they would send it with zero edits.
qs.a: Inside Harvey: How a First-Year Legal Associate Built One of Silicon Valley's Hottest Startups · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: So today we're serving over 7,000 businesses around the world and people are reporting up to  85 % time savings on contract review.
qs.a: Ep 301: From Law Student Startup Founder to Global CEO: Daniel Lewis's Legal Tech Journey · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

kps.k: Implementation should begin with bounded, repeatable workflows and explicit escalation criteria.
kps.d: The practical implication is to distinguish customer demand from work that can be delivered reliably and repeatedly. Teams should select tasks with defined inputs and outputs, connect relevant legal and organisational context, establish security and data controls, and specify when a lawyer must intervene. They should evaluate substantive quality alongside economics and usage rather than infer success from adoption alone. Broader agentic services and access-to-justice gains remain conditional on equivalent quality, effective supervision, regulatory compliance and whether lower costs or added capacity reach end users.

qs.q: I think it's really easy to confound like PMF of like your customer is asking you to do this thing and we'll pay you to do this thing versus like being an actual services business like you need to actually understand what is automatable, what is repeatable.
qs.a: Ryan Daniels & John Sarihan (Crosby) — Sequoia Training Data Ep.61 · AI-native providers · 2026

qs.q: So each stage has got pretty clearly defined inputs, pretty clearly defined outputs.
qs.a: Philip Young — Garfield AI: SRA Authorisation, Volume Economics, and the Access-to-Justice Case · AI-native providers · 2026

vlens.an: The curated AI-native legal-provider sources generally accept the proposition’s core: generative AI is most useful when embedded in contextual, task-specific legal workflows shaped by practising lawyers, with human judgment, supervision or escalation retained where risk requires it. They materially extend that proposition by arguing that the workflow layer should often be embodied in a provider that directly delivers completed legal work—not merely in software sold to incumbent firms. Their recurring reasons are that operating the service exposes tacit workflows and automation boundaries, aligns technology with client outcomes, enables close lawyer–engineer iteration, and permits the provider to assume regulated responsibility or liability. They commonly favour bounded, repeatable work, including contracts, funds work and small-debt recovery; some broaden the design to intake, billing and other whole-firm operations. Material variation concerns the intended depth and locus of automation. Crosby, Lawhive, Covenant and Soxton generally retain lawyers for direction, supervision, specialist judgment or escalation, although they pursue substantially greater automation than a conventional copilot. Garfield applies the thesis to a narrowly structured access-to-justice workflow through a regulated firm. By contrast, General Legal more clearly redirects the route to transformation away from tools retrofitted into incumbents and toward firms rebuilt on an AI foundation; Covenant also anticipates software-only delivery for some low-end contracting. The sources therefore develop rather than reject the proposition, but place greater emphasis on accountable service delivery and business-model redesign than its software-oriented title suggests. Their support is predominantly founder experience, design reasoning and forecasts; disclosed evidence rarely establishes comparative quality, realised economics or client outcomes.

qs.q: We believe that you need to go direct to clients and we believe that you need to embed legal expertise into the process um at different points.
qs.a: Jen Berrent — Covenant (founder) on what makes a firm 'AI-first' · AI-native providers · 2025

qs.q: There are, like—and, you know, I can get into hot takes on what kinds of legal work is going to be fully automated, but I think the key here is knowing exactly when to escalate something up to a lawyer and to get their thumbs up, and to know that that liability is covered.
qs.a: Deal Velocity, Not Billable Hours: How Crosby Uses AI to Redefine Legal Contracting — publisher's transcript · AI-native providers · 2025

vlens.an: This curated access-to-justice and civil-society evidence generally accepts the proposition that specialist value comes from contextual, task-specific layers around general-purpose models and materially extends it into legal-aid delivery. One source argues that an LLM requires complementary legal data structures, such as models of relationships among cases, reinforcing the case for specialist architecture. Another translates the workflow thesis into a bounded legal-aid use case: statewide intake, pre-screening and referral, with a low-cost path from experimentation to a client-facing application. These contributions remain prospective: they provide no measured outcomes and do not establish reliability, human verification arrangements or improved access to justice in operation. Material internal variation comes from Sateesh Nori, who redirects from software architecture to the underlying justice gap and the limitations of conventional legal-aid delivery; his account supplies the service rationale for innovation but neither evaluates AI nor proposes a concrete technical system. Thus, the professional voice builds on the cluster chiefly by identifying access-to-justice applications and necessary legal-data layers, while retaining a service-first strand that does not endorse the technology proposition itself.

qs.q: The last thing that I’ll say on this is that when it comes to building AI products that have legal utility, what you’re seeing in law but also in other fields is that it’s not enough just to have the large language model.
qs.a: Preventing Harm Amidst the AI Hype — full episode transcript · Access to justice · 2025

qs.q: So that is sort of low hanging fruit for us to use AI to do some of that pre-screening, to filter out people who don’t necessarily need to be in our process because they may not be eligible or it’s not the right sort of help for them and redirect ’em to the best sort of help.
qs.a: AI for Self-Help and Legal Aid at the Innovations in Technology Conference — full episode transcript · Access to justice · 2024

vlens.an: The selected in-house counsel and legal-operations sources accept the proposition that generative AI broadens the legal work software can address and that value depends on fitting the technology to legal context and workflow. Collectively, they build on it through a buyer-side implementation perspective: adoption begins with business needs, confidential or institutional data, bounded repeatable tasks and retained attorney accountability. Material variation lies in evidentiary strength. Klinger presents prospective self-service contract applications and confidentiality concerns rather than measured deployment; the Ford source offers an experiential comparison with earlier AI and an unquantified near-term ROI claim; Darr provides the strongest concrete extension, describing an LLM trained on ten years of internal EEOC position statements, with the signing attorney performing quality control and a reported—but not independently evaluated—80% time saving. These curated sources therefore reinforce contextual, verified copilot deployment, but do not establish general accuracy, durable ROI or the superiority of specialist workflow layers across legal work.

qs.q: Then the attorney who's signing comes in as quality control, right?
qs.a: Elaine Darr — DHL Supply Chain (VP Legal & Regulatory Affairs) on legal ops, trained models, and market-rate billing enforcement · In-house counsel · 2025

vlens.an:
The curated legal-tech-vendor sources accept the cluster’s principal proposition and materially extend it. Their common argument is that stronger foundation models broaden the legal work software can address, but durable specialist value lies in the surrounding workflow layer: authoritative and client-specific data, document and matter context, retrieval, integrations, permissions, security, evaluation, and interfaces embedded in lawyers’ existing systems. They add that this layer must be developed through close collaboration among practising lawyers, engineers, product managers, data scientists and customers. Most sources describe current deployment as a copilot model: lawyers direct tasks, verify outputs and retain professional accountability, while more autonomous or agentic operation remains concentrated in bounded workflows or framed as an emerging ambition.

There is material internal variation over where specialist value will persist. Some sources favour broad, model-agnostic assistants and orchestration platforms; others emphasise narrow practice-specific products, curated information layers, firm-specific workflow harnesses or in-house legal operating systems. Some anticipate client-tailored agents and greater automation, while governance-oriented sources prioritise quality assurance and supervision. A minority redirects attention toward general models absorbing simpler specialist features, well-resourced firms building internally, buyer-side management of legal work, or service commoditisation. These differences qualify—but do not displace—the shared view that contextual workflow systems presently add value above general models. The supporting evidence is mainly founder experience, product-development reasoning, demonstrations and customer anecdotes, not independent comparative proof of reliability, average productivity or client outcomes. Because the sources are curated, this conclusion characterises only the supplied vendor voice and is not a claim about prevalence across the sector.

qs.q: And I think you just very quickly found the rough edges of these models and just the sheer amount of product that you needed to build around them of how do we connect this to our data?
qs.a: Winston Weinberg & Gabe Pereyra — Harvey (co-founders): from roommates to 'essential infrastructure' · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: It's the work where lawyers and data scientists and product managers and engineers are teaching each other, learning from each other.
qs.a: Ep 287: From Ravel Cofounder to Knowable CEO, Nik Reed Has Learned that Building Quality AI for Legal Takes A Lot of Hard Work · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

vlens.an: This curated set of market analysts, consultancies and press sources broadly accepts the proposition that legal AI’s defensible value lies in contextual, workflow-specific systems surrounding foundation models. Common reasons include legal work’s dependence on nuanced text and process knowledge; the need for lawyers and engineers or legal technologists to define work products and map actual workflows; and the importance of data access, permissions, evaluation, governance and human handling of final outputs. The sources materially extend the proposition by describing concrete architectures that chain narrow capabilities or agents into integrated workflows, making specialist investment conditional on task-level ROI, and connecting workflow systems to fixed-fee services, firm-level infrastructure and AI-native delivery models. Material variation remains: some investment-focused sources establish only that LLMs fit legal work or have renewed investor interest, without resolving specialist-layer durability; one source redirects toward labour substitution and changing UPL boundaries; and Sean West directly challenges specialist defensibility by arguing that general-purpose AI may reproduce specialised features and weaken valuations. Even supportive accounts generally rely on product experience, demonstrations, anecdotes and forecasts rather than independent comparative evidence, and they vary in how strongly they retain the verified-copilot model versus anticipating agents or AI-delivered legal work.

qs.q: However, Weinberg argues that Harvey's focus on hiring lawyers as domain experts and integrating them with Harvey engineers, has helped them get the most out of the AI models they use (which besides OpenAI include Anthropic's Claude and models from Mistral and Xai).
qs.a: Legal AI startup Harvey lands fresh $300 million in Sequoia-led round · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: So basically, every AI company I've met in the legal space at some point has realized our software is not enough.
qs.a: E28 - Zach and Richard's Excellent Legal AI Adventure: Inside Eudia's Groundbreaking AI-First Law Firm · Market & press · 2025

vlens.an: Across this curated set, the sources generally accept the proposition that legal AI’s practical value depends on more than the underlying foundation model and materially develop its workflow and governance dimensions. Common reasoning centres on connecting AI to authoritative or organisation-specific context, integrating multi-step legal processes, and supplying enterprise controls such as security, privacy, ethical walls and regulatory safeguards. Fleisher gives the clearest account of a specialist workflow layer, linking documents, people, companies and prior deal history to support drafting and review; Pereyra adds the infrastructure required for deployment at organisational scale; Leonard and McCormack support the narrower case for language fit and legal or institutional data; and the SRA panel extends the account toward agentic workflows that connect research, synthesis, contextual retrieval and drafting. Material variation concerns whether specialist legal products will retain the surrounding value: the Legalweek source redirects attention toward organisations building directly on frontier-model stacks, with legal teams serving as governance pathfinders rather than relying on products such as Harvey or Legora. The sources also provide limited direct evidence for the synthesis’s lawyer–engineer collaboration and human-verification claims, and their deployment and performance observations are mainly experiential, anecdotal or predictive rather than comparative measurements. These positions describe only the supplied sources, not regulators, courts or professional bodies generally.

qs.q: And let's build a platform that doesn't just connect contracts to counterparties, but rather every document to every person, to every company, so that when we're actually using AI, we always can surface the right context immediately.
qs.a: How AI Is Reshaping In-House Legal Teams with Nick Fleisher — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: A lot of the product and platform problems you need to solve are not just, “How do you build a good product for an individual lawyer?”  It’s all of the security, data, privacy, governance, ethical walls—all of the regulatory challenges—everything you need so that a large law firm can use this with confidence.
qs.a: Harvey's Gabe Pereyra on the Future of Legal AI · Regulators & courts · 2026

vlens.an: The selected traditional-practice voices overall support the proposition, chiefly through concrete accounts of specialist workflow layers and governed, lawyer-facing adoption. LawPro.ai describes a multi-stage system for converting heterogeneous medical records into structured, task-specific information; Dentons presents a confidential GPT-4 layer for client work; and Quinn Emanuel emphasises hands-on experimentation, real-work collaboration, organisational culture and risk awareness. These accounts commonly locate value outside the foundation model itself—in workflow design, safeguards, user guidance, technical partnerships and implementation within the firm. Material internal variation remains: the startup-partnership, early-LLM and lawyer-education sources support only peripheral propositions about GPT-4’s significance, surprising general-model capability, technical expertise and early adoption, without taking a position on specialist-layer durability or verified copilot deployment. Even the more directly supportive sources generally do not document human verification practices, comparative accuracy or client outcomes, and their performance and safety claims are largely anecdotal or self-reported. Thus, the evidence supports the synthesis as an implementation direction rather than establishing its comparative or operational effectiveness. Because these are curated examples, this conclusion describes their relationship to the proposition and does not imply prevalence across traditional law firms.

qs.q: There's about 10 to 12 different processes the medical records and bills go through in our system on the back end, including we have something called hallucination prevention technology that's patent pending right now.
qs.a: E44 - Building a Law Firm and a Product: LawPro.ai Co-Founder and Zirkin Schmerling Partner, Josh Schmerling · Law firms · 2026

qs.q: The platform essentially allows us to use GPT4 on our client work in a safe, confidential manner – both for chat and for document upload.
qs.a: Joe Cohen on Dentons' fleetAI: 'It Gives Unique Perspectives' · Law firms · 2023

elens.an: The curated 2023–2024 sources support the proposition that the generative-AI shock broadened legal software’s reach while reinforcing the value of contextual workflow layers and lawyer-facing copilots. Their common reasoning is that GPT-4-class models made language-intensive tasks such as drafting, summarisation, contract analysis and information extraction newly tractable, but useful deployment still required bounded use cases, legal or institutional context, security and confidentiality controls, integration into existing work, practitioner feedback and demonstrated customer value. Firm and vendor accounts describe phased governance, task-specific applications and AI outputs used to inform lawyer decisions rather than replace judgment. Material variation remains. Harvey’s account favours custom legal models, whereas Ironclad advocates model-agnostic selection combined with retrieval and improved datasets; Robin AI forecasts eventual use both alongside and instead of lawyers, while Ironclad more explicitly presents decision support. The legal-aid source builds on the proposition by extending bounded workflows to intake, screening and referral, but only prospectively. Evidence strength is also uneven: reported uptake, development acceleration, lawyer preferences and accuracy claims are predominantly self-reported and often lack independent testing, comparative baselines or measured client outcomes. Several sources discuss safeguards without establishing systematic human verification, and some make broader access, substitution or return-on-investment predictions that exceed their evidence. Overall, the period strongly corroborates the workflow-layer and copilot direction, but not the reliability, durable commercial advantage or realised social benefits of those systems.

qs.q: Now, if that company is using AI Assist, and you’re a new attorney and you get a red line back, instead of asking the senior lawyer, you would ask AI Assist, “How does this company normally respond to that type of red line?” And it would respond, “Normally, this company would never agree to this or that.” I want to be clear here: AI Assist is not advising you to agree to this or that.
qs.a: Assisting Knowledge Workers · Legal-tech vendor · 2023

elens.an: The curated 2025 sources broadly accept the synthesis’s core proposition and materially develop it from a product thesis into an account of adoption at scale. Common reasons are that general models become legally useful only when surrounded by matter and client data, authoritative content, structured workflows, system integrations, permissions, security and legal-quality evaluation; adoption also requires accessible interfaces, practitioner-led iteration, training and organisational support. Many sources retain a verified-copilot model in which lawyers direct, review or approve outputs and remain professionally accountable. Concrete extensions include firm-wide workflow infrastructure, multi-step agents, in-house self-service, task-specific model orchestration and AI-native law firms or regulated services delivering completed outcomes. Internal variation is material: some favour broad assistants followed by specialised modules, while others prioritise narrow vertical workflows or structured-data products; software vendors generally complement incumbent firms, whereas Crosby, Covenant and Garfield pursue integrated or direct legal-service delivery. Agentic autonomy ranges from emerging supervised workflows to a longer-term goal, and Sean West directly challenges specialist defensibility by arguing that general-purpose AI may substitute for legal applications and eventually practise law under changed regulation. Other sources redirect toward access to justice, buyer-side advice management or service-price transparency, while several provide too little evidence on the proposition. Overall, the period builds on rather than merely repeats the proposition because it supplies concrete architectures, implementation models and limited operational examples. However, most adoption, performance and ROI claims remain founder-, vendor- or practitioner-reported anecdotes; the selected sources do not establish representative adoption, uniform reliability or settled comparative superiority.

qs.q: “We think of a lot of the product as not going to be the models, it’s going to be all of the infrastructure around them,” Pereyra noted.
qs.a: Lessons from Slush 2025: How Harvey Is Scaling Domain-Specific AI for Legal and Beyond · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: Then the attorney who's signing comes in as quality control, right?
qs.a: Elaine Darr — DHL Supply Chain (VP Legal & Regulatory Affairs) on legal ops, trained models, and market-rate billing enforcement · In-house counsel · 2025

elens.an:
The curated 2026 sources collectively build on the proposition rather than merely restating it. Their common starting point is that stronger language models have widened the range of tractable legal tasks, but that usable and defensible systems require substantial application-layer work: authoritative or client-specific data, persistent matter context, citations, document handling, integrations, security, permissions and workflow orchestration. Several sources materially develop the proposition with concrete mechanisms, including context graphs for in-house teams, firm-specific AI harnesses, synthetic transaction datasets with planted issues, lawyer-designed benchmarks, document-aware memory, workflow-specific agents and operating platforms spanning intake and administration. They also reinforce lawyer–engineer collaboration through embedded development teams, practitioner-led process mapping and rapid customer feedback. Human verification and professional accountability remain important in many accounts, particularly through explicit escalation, lawyer approval, regulated supervision and retained malpractice liability.

Material internal variation concerns where this specialist layer will reside and how autonomous it should become. Software vendors generally favour legal-specific copilots and enterprise infrastructure, whereas AI-native law firms and other legal-service providers argue that operating the service itself enables deeper workflow redesign and accountable delivery. Other sources redirect toward direct frontier-model use, internal law-firm development, lawyer-built bespoke applications or labour substitution, challenging the assumption that external specialist vendors will capture the value. Agent advocates foresee persistent-context systems running tasks in parallel with less supervision, while more cautious accounts retain lawyers for judgment-sensitive work. One source also argues that capabilities formerly distinctive to specialist research software are now essentially free through general models, directly qualifying claims of durable differentiation. Across these variants, however, the recurring extension is that differentiation must move beyond basic model access toward harder contextual, operational and governance problems.

The evidentiary base remains limited. Most support comes from founder experience, product demonstrations, customer anecdotes, reported adoption and company-supplied metrics rather than independent comparative evaluation. Predictions about agentic autonomy, AI-native firms, labour substitution and durable competitive advantage should therefore be treated as forecasts, not established outcomes.

qs.q: And I think you just very quickly found the rough edges of these models and just the sheer amount of product that you needed to build around them of how do we connect this to our data?
